defaults.permitted_development: Across Buckinghamshire, the key approval for a dropped kerb is normally the council or highway authority vehicle-crossing process. Planning permission can still be needed in some cases, especially on classified roads, in conservation areas, for listed buildings or where the frontage parking arrangement is not planning-compliant. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: Across Buckinghamshire, there is no simple height allowance for a dropped kerb. Problems usually arise where the site needs substantial engineered level changes to make vehicle access work.
rules.depth_rules: Across Buckinghamshire, dropped kerb can be refused or need redesign where the site does not provide workable off-street parking.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Buckinghamshire, the real decision point is usually at the boundary with the public highway, not on the paving inside the plot. Access geometry and road safety often matter more than the hardstanding alone.
rules.roof_rules: Across Buckinghamshire, a dropped kerb does not authorise a car port or canopy. Covered parking features belong under separate planning rules.
rules.materials_rules: Across Buckinghamshire, use the access and the driveway as one design problem: the parking surface should take run-off within the site and be robust enough for regular vehicle use rather than simply creating a widened opening onto the road.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status usually makes a new access more sensitive where it removes historic boundary features or changes a traditional frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Works to form an access for a listed building often need a heritage check as well as highways approval, especially where original frontage features are affected.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or an old planning condition can remove normal householder rights for frontage and access changes, even where the dropped kerb itself still needs separate highway consent.

rules.permitted_development: Lowering a kerb is not usually treated as a simple DIY householder project. The highway authority normally controls the crossing itself, and a planning application may still be needed if the site sits on a classified road or the associated hardstanding and frontage works fall outside the normal rules. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: There is no simple height allowance for a dropped kerb. Problems usually arise where the site needs substantial engineered level changes to make vehicle access work.
rules.depth_rules: The linked parking space must work safely in practice. Vehicles should be able to stand clear of the footway.
rules.boundary_rules: The real decision point is usually at the boundary with the public highway, not on the paving inside the plot. Access geometry and road safety often matter more than the hardstanding alone.
rules.roof_rules: A dropped kerb does not authorise a car port or canopy. Covered parking features belong under separate planning rules.
rules.materials_rules: Use the access and the driveway as one design problem: the parking surface should take run-off within the site and be robust enough for regular vehicle use rather than simply creating a widened opening onto the road.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status usually makes a new access more sensitive where it removes historic boundary features or changes a traditional frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: A new crossing serving a listed building can need listed building consent where boundary walls, gates, steps, railings or other historic fabric are altered.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the highway licence is the only approval needed: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions can still require a planning application for linked frontage or access works.
